intro: BMP to JPG converts BMP bitmaps, the classic Windows and Paint format, into JPG. A BMP stores every pixel uncompressed and an ordinary picture can take up tens of megabytes; the same content as JPG fits in a small part of that space and can be emailed or uploaded to any website.
Files are processed in your browser, without going through any server. Drop one or many BMP files: each JPG downloads separately and, if there are several, in a ZIP too.

JPG quality ranges from 1 to 100 and sits at 90, enough for no visible difference in photos and scans. For drawings with flat colours, text or screenshots it may be worth raising it a little to avoid halos around the edges.
Some 32-bit BMP files include transparency. JPG does not support it, so those areas are painted with the background colour you choose; if you change nothing, they are filled with white.

faq.q: How much space will I save?
faq.a: It depends on the image, but for photos or scans the JPG usually weighs a small fraction of the BMP. For drawings with large single-colour areas the saving is even bigger.

faq.q: Is the JPG exactly the same as the BMP?
faq.a: Not quite: JPG uses lossy compression. At quality 90 the difference is almost impossible to see; if you need a pixel-perfect copy, convert to PNG with Convert image.

faq.q: Can I turn a BMP into a PDF document?
faq.a: Yes, BMP to PDF places one or more BMP images on the pages of a PDF.
